name: Network Latency
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Why the Speed of Light Sets a Budget for Consensus
lesson.summary: Network latency, the unavoidable delay for data to travel between nodes, shapes core blockchain design choices like block time, because it determines how often independent participants act on stale information.
lesson.body:
Every distributed system has to grapple with a basic physical fact: information does not travel instantly. A node in one part of the world learns about a new block or transaction only after that data has physically propagated across the network, hop by hop, through however many intermediate peers happen to relay it. That delay is network latency, and it is shaped by physical distance, the speed of light through fiber optic cable, the processing time at each intermediate node, and the sheer size of the data being sent. None of these constraints are unique to blockchains; they are inherited from the broader reality of distributed systems, where no participant has instantaneous access to a single shared, up-to-the-millisecond view of the world.

For a blockchain built on proof-of-work mining, latency is not just an inconvenience, it actively shapes how often the network experiences forks. Recall that a fork can occur when two miners find valid blocks nearly simultaneously without knowing about each other's success. The more time it takes for a new block to reach the entire network, the larger the window during which a second miner could unknowingly be racing to solve the same puzzle on top of the same parent block. High latency relative to block time therefore produces more forks, more orphaned blocks, and more wasted mining effort, since work spent on a block that ultimately gets discarded under the longest chain rule earns nothing.

This is a major reason why block time cannot simply be set arbitrarily fast. A network that produced a new block every few seconds would see a much higher proportion of those blocks orphaned, because a meaningful fraction of the target interval would be consumed just by propagation delay rather than by genuine computational competition. Bitcoin's roughly ten-minute target block time is, among other things, a deliberate buffer against global network latency: it gives a newly found block enough time to reach the overwhelming majority of nodes worldwide before the next block is likely to be found, keeping fork rates low.

Real measurements of block propagation on major proof-of-work networks have generally found that blocks reach most of the network within seconds to a couple of minutes, depending on block size and how well-connected the relaying nodes are, which is a small fraction of a ten-minute interval but far from instantaneous. Designers of faster blockchains have had to invest specifically in propagation techniques, such as sending compact block representations instead of full transaction data, precisely to keep latency from eating into their shorter target intervals.

The underlying lesson generalizes well beyond mining specifics: any distributed system that needs independent participants to agree on an ordering of events has to budget for the fact that participants are working from slightly different, slightly delayed pictures of reality. Latency is not a bug introduced by sloppy engineering, it is a physical constraint that consensus protocols must be explicitly designed around, and blockchain block-time choices are one of the clearest visible traces of that design pressure.
